claim: The LRRK2 G2019S mutation is one of the most common genetic determinants associated with an increased risk to develop sporadic or familial Parkinson's disease.
source: The LRRK2 G2019S mutation is one of the most common genetic determinants associated with an increased risk to develop sporadic or familial PD (Bonifati, 2006; Kumari and Tan, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Bonifati, 2006; Kumari and Tan, 2009)

claim: iPSC-derived astrocytes express the markers GFAP, vimentin, and CD44.
source: As expected, astrocytes expressed the markers GFAP, vimentin, and CD44 as demonstrated by immunofluorescence (Figure 1A) and flow cytometry analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence imaging (Figure 1A) and flow cytometry data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)

claim: 100% of differentiated astrocytes express GFAP in both WT and LRRK2 G2019S cells.
source: Differentiation was equally effective in WT and LRRK2 G2019S cells, with 100% of the differentiated astrocytes expressing GFAP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2Bi).
evidence: Quantitative data from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2Bi

claim: Principal component and unsupervised cluster analyses separated undifferentiated iPSCs, iPSC-derived NPCs, and iPSC-derived astrocytes into independent clusters.
source: In addition, principal component and unsupervised cluster analyses separated undifferentiated iPSCs, iPSC-derived NPCs, and iPSC-derived astrocytes into independent clusters, demonstrating that our differentiation strategy produces distinct cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: RNA-seq data analyzed by principal component analysis and unsupervised clustering shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D

claim: The transcriptome of iPSC-derived astrocytes shows more similarities to fetal human midbrain astrocytes than to NPCs or iPSCs.
source: Importantly, the transcriptome of iPSC-derived astrocytes showed more similarities to fetal human midbrain astrocytes than to NPCs or iPSCs, further validating their astrocyte identity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: RNA-seq transcriptomic comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D

claim: Control and LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes show classic astrocytic functional phenotypes such as spontaneous and transient calcium signaling and synaptosome uptake.
source: Lastly, control and LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes showed classic astrocytic functional phenotypes such as spontaneous and transient calcium signaling and synaptosome uptake (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: Functional assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and F demonstrate calcium signaling and synaptosome uptake

claim: Differential gene expression analysis revealed that the isogenic pair differed by a total of 348 genes.
source: Differential gene expression analysis revealed that the isogenic pair differed by a total of 348 genes (Figure 1B), and the non-isogenic pair by 563 genes.
evidence: RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1B

claim: The non-isogenic pair differed by 563 genes.
source: Differential gene expression analysis revealed that the isogenic pair differed by a total of 348 genes (Figure 1B), and the non-isogenic pair by 563 genes.
evidence: RNA-seq differential expression analysis

claim: Gene ontology analysis revealed that components of the extracellular compartment are highly upregulated and include the extracellular region, extracellular matrix, and extracellular exosomes.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis revealed that components of the extracellular compartment are highly upregulated and include the extracellular region, extracellular matrix, and extracellular exosomes (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: GO analysis results shown in Figure 1D and F

claim: The exosome component is one of the most significantly upregulated GO terms in both isogenic and non-isogenic astrocytes.
source: The exosome component is one of the most significantly upregulated GO terms in both isogenic and non-isogenic astrocytes, and comprises a total of 67 (isogenic pair) or 95 (non-isogenic pair) genes (Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: GO analysis of RNA-seq data with quantification of genes in exosome component

claim: RAB27B expression shows a 5-fold increase in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes compared to WT astrocytes.
source: Quantification of gene expression by RT-qPCR showed a 5-fold increase in RAB27B (associated with exosome trafficking) and a 64-fold increase in CD82 (associated with exosome biogenesis) (Andreu and Yáñez-Mó, 2014; Chiasserini et al., 2014; Ostrowski et al., 2010), in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes compared to WT astrocytes (Figure 1E, G and H).
evidence: RT-qPCR quantification shown in Figure 1E, G and H, with citations supporting the functional roles of these genes

claim: CD82 expression shows a 64-fold increase in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes compared to WT astrocytes.
source: Quantification of gene expression by RT-qPCR showed a 5-fold increase in RAB27B (associated with exosome trafficking) and a 64-fold increase in CD82 (associated with exosome biogenesis) (Andreu and Yáñez-Mó, 2014; Chiasserini et al., 2014; Ostrowski et al., 2010), in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes compared to WT astrocytes (Figure 1E, G and H).
evidence: RT-qPCR quantification shown in Figure 1E, G and H, with citations supporting the functional roles of these genes

claim: Both WT and LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes produce MVB-like structures.
source: We found that while both WT and LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes produce MVBs (Figure 2A), their average size is genotype-dependent.
evidence: TEM images in Figure 2A show MVBs in both genotypes

claim: The average area of MVBs in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes is 0.26 µm2.
source: The area of MVBs in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes is smaller than in WT astrocytes, with an average of 0.26 µm2 (SEM = 0.02079) in LRRK2 G2019S and 0.44 µm2 (SEM = 0.03472) in WT cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Quantitative TEM analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: The average area of MVBs in WT astrocytes is 0.44 µm2.
source: The area of MVBs in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes is smaller than in WT astrocytes, with an average of 0.26 µm2 (SEM = 0.02079) in LRRK2 G2019S and 0.44 µm2 (SEM = 0.03472) in WT cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Quantitative TEM analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: MVBs with an area smaller than 0.2 µm2 are over-represented in LRRK2 G2019S compared to WT astrocytes.
source: MVBs with an area smaller than 0.2 µm2 are over-represented in LRRK2 G2019S compared to WT astrocytes, which range in area from 0.1 to 1.2 µm2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Size distribution analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: CD63-positive MVBs are present in iPSC-derived isogenic astrocytes.
source: We therefore confirmed the presence of CD63-positive MVBs in iPSC-derived isogenic astrocytes by immunofluorescence (Figure 2D) and immunogold electron microscopy (IEM) (Figure 2E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence (Figure 2D) and IEM (Figure 2E) demonstrate CD63+ MVBs

claim: WT and LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes have similar levels of CD63 localized within MVBs.
source: Analysis of IEM images showed an abundance and similar level of CD63 localized within MVBs in WT and LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes (Figure 2E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), confirming that CD63 can be used as a marker of MVBs and exosomes in iPSC-derived astrocytes.
evidence: IEM quantification shown in Figure 2E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: iPSC-derived astrocytes actively produce and secrete EVs by exocytosis.
source: We first analyzed iPSC-derived astrocytes by TEM and confirmed the presence of EVs that appear to be secreted by exocytosis (Figure 3A), and by a mechanism that resembles membrane budding or shedding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: TEM images in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C show EVs being secreted

claim: The astrocyte-derived EV pellet is enriched in exosomes, as demonstrated by the expression of eight exosomal markers and the absence of cellular contamination.
source: The astrocyte-derived EV pellet is enriched in exosomes, as demonstrated by the expression of eight exosomal markers and the absence of cellular contamination (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Exosome marker array shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: The number of secreted EVs does not differ between LRRK2 G2019S and isogenic control.
source: NTA quantification showed that the number of secreted EVs does not differ between LRRK2 G2019S and isogenic control (Figure 3C), and it appears that LRRK2 G2019S particles have a slightly different size distribution compared to WT particles (Figure 3D).
evidence: NTA quantification shown in Figure 3C

claim: LRRK2 G2019S particles have a slightly different size distribution compared to WT particles.
source: NTA quantification showed that the number of secreted EVs does not differ between LRRK2 G2019S and isogenic control (Figure 3C), and it appears that LRRK2 G2019S particles have a slightly different size distribution compared to WT particles (Figure 3D).
evidence: NTA size distribution analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: WT astrocyte-secreted EVs display a large range of sizes, from 80 nm to greater than 600 nm in diameter.
source: Cryo-EM analysis confirmed that WT astrocyte-secreted EVs display a large range of sizes, from 80 nm to greater than 600 nm in diameter, with differences between WT and mutant populations (Figure 3F).
evidence: Cryo-EM size analysis shown in Figure 3F

claim: Mutant astrocytes secreted fewer particles in the 0–120 nm size range according to cryo-EM data.
source: The cryo-EM data suggested that mutant astrocytes secreted fewer particles in the 0–120 nm size range.
evidence: Cryo-EM size distribution analysis

claim: Multiple EV structures represent up to 16% of the EV population.
source: Quantification of the number of simple vs. multiple EV structures did not reveal differences between the mutant and WT, and represent up to 16% of the EV population (Figure 3G).
evidence: Cryo-EM morphology quantification shown in Figure 3G

claim: The number of CD63+ EVs remained unchanged between WT and LRRK2 G2019S genotypes.
source: We previously showed that WT and LRRK2 G2019S MVBs contain similar levels of the CD63 tetraspanin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), and an ELISA-based quantification confirmed that the number of CD63+ EVs remained unchanged between the two genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: ELISA quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F

claim: The proportion of LRRK2+/CD63+ structures remains unchanged between WT and LRRK2 G2019S isogenic astrocytes.
source: We analyzed and quantified the colocalization of LRRK2 with CD63 (Figure 4A), a marker for MVBs (Beatty, 2008; Edgar et al., 2014), and found that the proportion of LRRK2+/CD63+ structures remains unchanged between WT and LRRK2 G2019S isogenic astrocytes (Figure 4B).
evidence: Colocalization analysis shown in Figure 4A and 4B, with citations supporting CD63 as MVB marker

claim: LRRK2 is localized both in the vicinity of and inside CD63+ MVBs.
source: To reveal the localization of LRRK2 in finer detail, we analyzed IEM images, which demonstrated that LRRK2 (small gold) is localized both in the vicinity of and inside CD63+ MVBs (large gold) (Figure 4C).
evidence: IEM images shown in Figure 4C

claim: 65% of MVBs in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes are LRRK2+/CD63+ vs. only 44% in WT astrocytes.
source: Importantly, small gold LRRK2 was more frequently localized inside MVBs in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes compared to WT astrocytes – 65% of MVBs in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes are LRRK2+/CD63+ vs. only 44% in WT astrocytes.
evidence: IEM quantification of LRRK2 localization in MVBs

claim: LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes contained an average of 1.8 LRRK2 small gold particles per MVB compared to only 0.9 small gold particles in WT astrocytes.
source: LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes contained an average of 1.8 LRRK2 small gold particles per MVB compared to only 0.9 small gold particles in WT astrocytes, and MVB populations containing more than five LRRK2 small gold particles were only observed in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes (Figure 4D).
evidence: IEM quantification shown in Figure 4D

claim: MVB populations containing more than five LRRK2 small gold particles were only observed in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes.
source: LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes contained an average of 1.8 LRRK2 small gold particles per MVB compared to only 0.9 small gold particles in WT astrocytes, and MVB populations containing more than five LRRK2 small gold particles were only observed in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes (Figure 4D).
evidence: IEM quantification shown in Figure 4D

claim: LRRK2 is present in EV-enriched fractions isolated from astrocyte conditioned media.
source: We then performed biochemical assays to determine if astrocytes secrete LRRK2 in EVs, and ELISA analysis confirmed the presence of LRRK2 in EV-enriched fractions isolated from ACM (Figure 4E).
evidence: ELISA quantification shown in Figure 4E

claim: The median distance of CD63+ MVBs to the nuclear membrane was 9.2 µm in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes compared to 4.8 µm in isogenic controls.
source: The median distance of CD63+ MVBs to the nuclear membrane was 9.2 µm in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes compared to 4.8 µm in isogenic controls, and 11.5 µm in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes compared to 7.5 µm in the non-isogenic control.
evidence: Quantitative immunofluorescence analysis of MVB distribution

claim: The median distance of CD63+ MVBs to the nuclear membrane was 11.5 µm in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes compared to 7.5 µm in the non-isogenic control.
source: The median distance of CD63+ MVBs to the nuclear membrane was 9.2 µm in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes compared to 4.8 µm in isogenic controls, and 11.5 µm in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes compared to 7.5 µm in the non-isogenic control.
evidence: Quantitative immunofluorescence analysis of MVB distribution

claim: 75% of the isogenic control CD63+ MVBs were localized at a distance to the nucleus smaller than 11.23 µm compared to 19.34 µm in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes.
source: Furthermore, 75% of the isogenic control CD63+ MVBs were localized at a distance to the nucleus smaller than 11.23 µm compared to 19.34 µm in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Quantitative immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 5B and C

claim: 75% of the non-isogenic control CD63+ MVBs were localized at a distance to the nucleus smaller than 15.82 µm compared to 23.79 µm in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes.
source: In non-isogenic lines, 75% of the control CD63+ MVBs were localized at a distance to the nucleus smaller than 15.82 µm compared to 23.79 µm in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Quantitative immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 5D and E

claim: 55% of the CD63+ MVBs in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes are also p-αSyn+, compared to only 16% in WT MVBs.
source: We observed that 55% of the CD63+ (large gold) MVBs in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes are also p-αSyn+ (small gold), compared to only 16% in WT MVBs.
evidence: IEM quantification of p-αSyn in MVBs

claim: LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes contained on average 1.3 p-αSyn small gold particles per MVB compared to only 0.16 small gold particles in isogenic control astrocytes.
source: LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes contained on average 1.3 p-αSyn small gold particles per MVB compared to only 0.16 small gold particles in isogenic control astrocytes, and MVB populations containing more than 3 p-αSyn small gold particles were only observed in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes (Figure 6B).
evidence: IEM quantification shown in Figure 6B

claim: MVB populations containing more than 3 p-αSyn small gold particles were only observed in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes.
source: LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes contained on average 1.3 p-αSyn small gold particles per MVB compared to only 0.16 small gold particles in isogenic control astrocytes, and MVB populations containing more than 3 p-αSyn small gold particles were only observed in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes (Figure 6B).
evidence: IEM quantification shown in Figure 6B

claim: Total αSyn levels in EV-enriched fractions are similar between isogenic controls and LRRK2 G2019S.
source: When we analyzed the content of EVs by ELISA, we found that total αSyn levels (phosphorylated and non-phosphorylated) in EV-enriched fractions are similar between isogenic controls and LRRK2 G2019S (Figure 6C).
evidence: ELISA quantification shown in Figure 6C

claim: On average, 40% of the dopaminergic neurons had internalized exosomes regardless of the astrocyte genotype.
source: We co-cultured dopaminergic neurons with either WT or G2019S astrocytes, but did not observe a difference in the proportion of exosome-containing neurons. On average, 40% of the dopaminergic neurons had internalized exosomes regardless of the astrocyte genotype (Figure 7C).
evidence: Live-cell confocal microscopy quantification shown in Figure 7C

claim: There was no difference in the amount of exosomes internalized by neurons exposed to either WT or LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes.
source: Although there was no difference in the amount of exosomes internalized by neurons exposed to either WT or LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes (Figure 7D), exosomes were significantly over-represented in the neurites of neurons exposed to LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 7D

claim: Exosomes were significantly over-represented in the neurites of neurons exposed to LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes.
source: Although there was no difference in the amount of exosomes internalized by neurons exposed to either WT or LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes (Figure 7D), exosomes were significantly over-represented in the neurites of neurons exposed to LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 7E and F

claim: The neuronal dendrites shortened from an average of 60 µm in WT to 45 µm in LRRK2 G2019S isogenic cultures.
source: The neuronal dendrites shortened from an average of 60 µm in WT to 45 µm in LRRK2 G2019S isogenic cultures (Figure 8C).
evidence: Dendrite length quantification shown in Figure 8C

claim: Co-culture of WT neurons with LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes resulted in loss of 37% more of the dopaminergic neurons than co-cultures containing WT astrocytes at 14 days.
source: A 14 days, co-culture of WT neurons with LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes resulted in loss of 37% more of the dopaminergic neurons than co-cultures containing WT astrocytes (Figure 8G and H).
evidence: Neuron viability quantification in mouse primary cultures shown in Figure 8G and H

claim: Neuronal death induced by LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes was selective for dopaminergic neurons.
source: Moreover, this neuronal death was selective for dopaminergic neurons (Figure 8I), recapitulating a key feature of PD.
evidence: Selective neuron viability quantification shown in Figure 8I

claim: LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes reduced the viability of LRRK2 G2019S dopaminergic neurons.
source: LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes also reduced the viability of LRRK2 G2019S dopaminergic neurons (Figure 8J), but did not affect non-dopaminergic neuronal populations (Figure 8K).
evidence: Neuron viability quantification shown in Figure 8J

claim: LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes did not affect non-dopaminergic neuronal populations.
source: LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes also reduced the viability of LRRK2 G2019S dopaminergic neurons (Figure 8J), but did not affect non-dopaminergic neuronal populations (Figure 8K).
evidence: Neuron viability quantification shown in Figure 8K

claim: The average dendrite length of dopaminergic neurons exposed to WT ACM was 64.4 µm compared to 50.3 µm if the dopaminergic neurons were exposed to basal NB/B27 medium.
source: After 14 days in culture, the average dendrite length of dopaminergic neurons exposed to WT ACM was 64.4 µm compared to 50.3 µm if the dopaminergic neurons were exposed to basal NB/B27 medium (Figure 9A).
evidence: Dendrite length quantification shown in Figure 9A

claim: WT ACM, but not basal medium, contains neurotrophic factors necessary for dendrite outgrowth.
source: This observation suggests that WT ACM, but not basal medium, contains neurotrophic factors necessary for dendrite outgrowth.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of dendrite lengths in different media conditions

claim: LRRK2 G2019S ACM resulted in a 26% increase in the number of short neurites (0–40 µm), and the absence of long neurites (160–200 µm) compared to neurons exposed to WT ACM.
source: LRRK2 G2019S ACM mimicked the phenotype observed by direct co-culture, with a 26% increase in the number of short neurites (0–40 µm), and the absence of long neurites (160–200 µm) compared to neurons exposed to WT ACM (Figure 9B).
evidence: Dendrite length distribution analysis shown in Figure 9B

claim: The average dendrite length of dopaminergic neurons cultured in basal medium is equivalent to those cultured in LRRK2 G2019S ACM (50.3 µm vs. 49.1 µm, respectively).
source: The average dendrite length of dopaminergic neurons cultured in basal medium or LRRK2 G2019S ACM is equivalent (50.3 µm vs. 49.1 µm, respectively) (Figure 9A).
evidence: Dendrite length quantification shown in Figure 9A

claim: WT EV-free medium promoted neuronal health, as evidenced by an average dendrite outgrowth of 60.3 µm compared to 51 µm in basal medium.
source: WT EV-free medium promoted neuronal health, as evidenced by an average dendrite outgrowth of 60.3 µm compared to 51 µm in basal medium (Figure 9E).
evidence: Dendrite length quantification shown in Figure 9E

claim: LRRK2 G2019S EV-free medium did not support dendrite outgrowth, as evidenced by an average length of 48.7 µm.
source: In contrast, LRRK2 G2019S EV-free medium did not support dendrite outgrowth, as evidenced by an average length of 48.7 µm.
evidence: Dendrite length quantification

claim: Soluble factors found in WT but not LRRK2 G2019S EV-free ACM mediate neuron growth.
source: We conclude that soluble factors found in WT but not LRRK2 G2019S EV-free ACM mediate neuron growth.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from dendrite length measurements in different media conditions

claim: WT EVs supported a 30% increase in dendrite length compared to basal medium.
source: WT EVs supported a 30% increase in dendrite length compared to basal medium (Figure 9G), which is higher than the 18% increase supported by WT soluble factors (Figure 9E).
evidence: Dendrite length quantification shown in Figure 9G

claim: WT soluble factors supported an 18% increase in dendrite length.
source: WT EVs supported a 30% increase in dendrite length compared to basal medium (Figure 9G), which is higher than the 18% increase supported by WT soluble factors (Figure 9E).
evidence: Dendrite length quantification shown in Figure 9E

claim: LRRK2 G2019S EVs supported an 11% increase in dendrite length.
source: Interestingly, LRRK2 G2019S EVs were not as efficient as their WT counterparts, but they supported a 11% increase in dendrite length (Figure 9G) and reduced the proportion of short neurites (0–40 µm) (Figure 9H).
evidence: Dendrite length quantification shown in Figure 9G

claim: WT astrocytes secrete neurotrophic factors not only via direct release into the extracellular compartment, but also via production and release of EVs.
source: These results suggest that WT astrocytes secrete neurotrophic factors not only via direct release into the extracellular compartment, but also via production and release of EVs.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of neurotrophic effects of EV-free and EV-enriched fractions

claim: Cholesterol biosynthetic processes are downregulated in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes in both isogenic and non-isogenic lines.
source: A GO analysis of downregulated genes in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes revealed a defect in cholesterol as well as isoprenoid biosynthetic processes (Figure 10A and B) in both isogenic and non-isogenic lines.
evidence: GO analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 10A and B

claim: Isoprenoid biosynthetic processes are downregulated in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes in both isogenic and non-isogenic lines.
source: A GO analysis of downregulated genes in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes revealed a defect in cholesterol as well as isoprenoid biosynthetic processes (Figure 10A and B) in both isogenic and non-isogenic lines.
evidence: GO analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 10A and B

claim: Genes associated with cell growth and survival were significantly downregulated in mutant astrocytes, including BIRC5, FLOT1, HTRA1, PAK1, KCNMA1, and LZTS1.
source: Furthermore, genes associated with cell growth and survival were significantly downregulated in mutant astrocytes, including BIRC5, FLOT1, HTRA1, PAK1, KCNMA1, and LZTS1 (Figure 10C).
evidence: RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 10C

claim: BIRC5, FLOT1, PAK1, and LZTS1 regulate neuronal growth.
source: These genes regulate neuronal growth (BIRC5, FLOT1, PAK1, LZTS1) and/or function (FLOT1, PAK1, LZTS1) (Contet et al., 2016; Du et al., 2020; Kawaue et al., 2019; Ko et al., 2011; Launay et al., 2008; Pan et al., 2015; Swanwick et al., 2010), and can be found in EVs (FLOT1, HTRA1, KCNMA1) (Skog et al., 2008), suggesting that they could be shuttled between neurons and astrocytes via this communication pathway.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations describing gene functions

claim: FLOT1, PAK1, and LZTS1 regulate neuronal function.
source: These genes regulate neuronal growth (BIRC5, FLOT1, PAK1, LZTS1) and/or function (FLOT1, PAK1, LZTS1) (Contet et al., 2016; Du et al., 2020; Kawaue et al., 2019; Ko et al., 2011; Launay et al., 2008; Pan et al., 2015; Swanwick et al., 2010), and can be found in EVs (FLOT1, HTRA1, KCNMA1) (Skog et al., 2008), suggesting that they could be shuttled between neurons and astrocytes via this communication pathway.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations describing gene functions

claim: FLOT1, HTRA1, and KCNMA1 can be found in EVs.
source: These genes regulate neuronal growth (BIRC5, FLOT1, PAK1, LZTS1) and/or function (FLOT1, PAK1, LZTS1) (Contet et al., 2016; Du et al., 2020; Kawaue et al., 2019; Ko et al., 2011; Launay et al., 2008; Pan et al., 2015; Swanwick et al., 2010), and can be found in EVs (FLOT1, HTRA1, KCNMA1) (Skog et al., 2008), suggesting that they could be shuttled between neurons and astrocytes via this communication pathway.
evidence: Supported by citation (Skog et al., 2008)

claim: The loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta is associated with the severe and debilitating motor dysfunction observed in Parkinson's disease patients.
source: The loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta is associated with the severe and debilitating motor dysfunction observed in Parkinson's disease (PD) patients (Massano and Bhatia, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation (Massano and Bhatia, 2012)

claim: Cellular stressors such as oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and disruption of protein degradation pathways play roles in dopaminergic neuron degeneration.
source: The cause of dopaminergic neuron degeneration has been under intense investigation and has revealed the roles played by cellular stressors such as oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and disruption of protein degradation pathways (Dawson and Dawson, 2003; Lynch-Day et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations (Dawson and Dawson, 2003; Lynch-Day et al., 2012)

claim: Astrocytes are specialized in detecting and responding to neuronal signals to support neuronal health and function.
source: Among these non-neuronal populations, astrocytes are specialized in detecting and responding to neuronal signals to support neuronal health and function (Allen and Eroglu, 2017; Banker, 1980), suggesting that impaired astrocytic functions could initiate or accelerate neuron loss.
evidence: Supported by citations (Allen and Eroglu, 2017; Banker, 1980)

claim: Neurons rely on astrocytes for regulation of their firing activities.
source: Neurons rely on astrocytes for regulation of their firing activities (Deemyad et al., 2018), for trophic and metabolic support (Allen and Lyons, 2018), and detoxification of harmful factors (Ioannou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation (Deemyad et al., 2018)

claim: Neurons rely on astrocytes for trophic and metabolic support.
source: Neurons rely on astrocytes for regulation of their firing activities (Deemyad et al., 2018), for trophic and metabolic support (Allen and Lyons, 2018), and detoxification of harmful factors (Ioannou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation (Allen and Lyons, 2018)

claim: Neurons rely on astrocytes for detoxification of harmful factors.
source: Neurons rely on astrocytes for regulation of their firing activities (Deemyad et al., 2018), for trophic and metabolic support (Allen and Lyons, 2018), and detoxification of harmful factors (Ioannou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation (Ioannou et al., 2019)

claim: Astrocytes can change from a resting to a reactive state in response to injury.
source: However, astrocytes can change from a resting to a reactive state in response to injury (Zamanian et al., 2012) or normal aging (Clarke et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation (Zamanian et al., 2012)

claim: Astrocytes can change from a resting to a reactive state in response to normal aging.
source: However, astrocytes can change from a resting to a reactive state in response to injury (Zamanian et al., 2012) or normal aging (Clarke et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation (Clarke et al., 2018)

claim: Depending on the nature of the extracellular signals released after injury, astrocytes can protect neurons or induce neurotoxicity.
source: In fact, depending on the nature of the extracellular signals released after injury, astrocytes can protect neurons or induce neurotoxicity (Liddelow et al., 2017; Zamanian et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations (Liddelow et al., 2017; Zamanian et al., 2012)

claim: Astrocytes with the ALS-causing mutation SOD1 G93A produced factors toxic to motor neurons.
source: For example, studies showed that astrocytes with the ALS-causing mutation SOD1 G93A produced factors toxic to motor neurons (Di Giorgio et al., 2008), as well as failed to secrete factors that support the viability of neurons (Basso et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation (Di Giorgio et al., 2008)

claim: Astrocytes with the ALS-causing mutation SOD1 G93A failed to secrete factors that support the viability of neurons.
source: For example, studies showed that astrocytes with the ALS-causing mutation SOD1 G93A produced factors toxic to motor neurons (Di Giorgio et al., 2008), as well as failed to secrete factors that support the viability of neurons (Basso et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation (Basso et al., 2013)

claim: Astrocytes with the LRRK2 G2019S mutation were found to alter neuronal morphology in a non-cell-autonomous fashion and shuttle detrimental astrocyte-derived alpha-synuclein to co-cultured neurons.
source: Similarly, astrocytes with the LRRK2 G2019S mutation were found to alter neuronal morphology in a non-cell-autonomous fashion and shuttle detrimental astrocyte-derived alpha-synuclein (αSyn) to co-cultured neurons (di Domenico et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation (di Domenico et al., 2019)

claim: Microvesicles are approximately 100 nm to 1 µm in diameter and are formed by budding of the plasma membrane directly into the extracellular space.
source: Microvesicles (~100 nm to 1 µm diameter) are formed by budding of the plasma membrane directly into the extracellular space, and their cargo resembles the cytoplasmic signature of the cell of origin (Pegtel and Gould, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation (Pegtel and Gould, 2019)

claim: Exosomes are approximately 40–120 nm in diameter and are formed by a regulated inward budding of early endosomes to form exosome-containing multivesicular bodies, as well as by budding of the plasma membrane.
source: Exosomes (~40–120 nm) are formed by a regulated inward budding of early endosomes to form exosome-containing multivesicular bodies (MVBs), as well as by budding of the plasma membrane (Pegtel and Gould, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation (Pegtel and Gould, 2019)

claim: The sorting and loading of exosome cargo is an active and regulated process.
